title: Long-distance relationships: 7 habits to feel closer every day
description: Seven practical ideas for a long-distance relationship: rituals, questions, shared moments and planning reunions, without pressure.
summary: To feel closer at a distance, choose a realistic small ritual, share ordinary moments and plan your next reunion together. Regular contact should remain an invitation: everyone can need time to themselves.

sections.title: 1. Find a rhythm that works for both of you
paragraphs: An internship abroad, studying in different cities or mismatched schedules can change when you connect. Start by explaining when you are available instead of expecting an immediate reply.
Try a ten-minute catch-up two or three evenings a week. After a week, adjust: does it feel enjoyable or like another obligation? A helpful habit leaves room for unexpected changes.

sections.title: 2. Replace an automatic question with real curiosity
paragraphs: ‘How are you?’ is sometimes enough, but may not open much conversation. Try ‘Which moment today would you have liked to share with me?’ Answer it yourself too, and listen without immediately trying to solve a problem.

sections.title: 3. Share something ordinary
paragraphs: A photo of lunch, a song from your bus ride or a small win at work gives you something to talk about beyond big updates. Pick a detail you want to share without turning your day into a report.

sections.title: 4. Plan a date at a distance
paragraphs: Cook the same recipe, watch an episode together or play a short game. Agree on a start time and approximate length. Afterwards, ask what you would like to do again: a good activity is one you both enjoy.

sections.title: 5. Make your next reunion tangible
paragraphs: Where possible, note the next visit date and choose something simple to do together. If your budget or schedule gets in the way, agree when to revisit the plan. A countdown can make waiting enjoyable without promising something you cannot deliver.

sections.title: 6. Keep a space for your memories
paragraphs: Gather a few moments in a shared album with a sentence about what they mean. When conversation runs dry, choose a memory and say what you would like to experience again. Ask before sharing an image outside your space.

sections.title: 7. Leave room for a pause
paragraphs: A late reply alone does not explain how your partner feels. Agree on a simple way to say ‘Busy day, I’ll catch up tomorrow.’ Questions, location sharing and activities should remain choices, never proof someone has to provide.

Nearly is designed to bring questions, moods, memories, a calendar and a reunion countdown into a private couple space. The app is coming soon to iOS and Android; you can already try couple questions on the website without an account.

faqs.question: Do long-distance couples need to talk every day?
faqs.answer: There is no single right frequency. Agree on a rhythm that fits your schedules and adjust if either person feels overlooked or pressured.

faqs.question: What can we do when we run out of conversation topics?
faqs.answer: Start with a memory, try an open question or suggest a short activity such as cooking the same recipe. A call can also feel good without constant conversation.

title: Couple questions: a five-minute ritual you will want to keep
description: A simple ritual and ten couple questions to move beyond ‘How are you?’, listen and share a moment, far apart or under the same roof.
summary: A couple ritual can take five minutes: one open question, an answer from each person and a small gesture afterwards. Choose a calm moment and always leave room to skip a question.

sections.title: A simple format to try tonight
paragraphs: Choose a question before you start. One person answers and the other listens, then swap. Finish by naming something you appreciated about the exchange. The aim is to discover a detail, not complete a list.
Try it out loud, on a walk or in writing if your schedules differ. Avoid a sensitive question when someone has to leave. If five minutes is not enough, suggest returning to it later.

sections.title: 10 questions to start without pressure
paragraphs: Choose according to your mood: not every conversation needs to be deep. A light question can be a good start after a long day.
bullets: What made you smile today?
What little moment would you like us to share this week?
Which song reminds you of us?
Which memory of us would you describe as a film scene?
What are you proud of at the moment?
What small gesture would make you happy this week?
What would you like to learn with me?
What would our ideal Sunday look like?
When do you feel most listened to?
What small adventure could we plan together?

sections.title: Listen before responding
paragraphs: An answer unlike yours is not a bad result. Ask ‘Would you like to tell me more?’ instead of comparing straight away. If your partner describes a difficulty, ask whether they want an idea or just someone to listen.
Agree that either person can skip a question. Avoid saving an answer to use as an argument later: the ritual works better when the exchange feels trustworthy.

sections.title: Continue with Nearly
paragraphs: Nearly plans a daily question, themed questions with a shared reveal and shared moods. These offer a starting point in your private space alongside memories and upcoming moments.
To start now, the website’s couple questions demo is free and needs no account. It is a limited preview; the full app is still coming soon. Try a question, then keep only the rhythm that suits you.

faqs.question: What questions can I ask my partner at a distance?
faqs.answer: Choose questions about daily life, memories or the next reunion. ‘Which moment would you have liked to share with me?’ is a simple starting point.

faqs.answer: Yes. The couple questions demo on the website is free and available without an account. It previews activities planned for the app.

title: Stay connected with friends and family when you live far apart
description: Easy ideas to stay close to friends and family at a distance: updates, private memories, games and relaxed catch-ups.
summary: To stay connected with loved ones, alternate small updates, memories and realistic catch-ups. A shared space helps you find those moments again; what matters is choosing habits everyone can access.

sections.title: Give updates a starting point
paragraphs: After a move, a group chat can fall silent without the friendships becoming less important. Suggest a relaxed habit: a Sunday photo or one good thing from the week. Explain that taking part is optional.

With family, choose a format that works for those less familiar with apps. A photo with one sentence can provide more context than a stream of pictures. Individual calls still have a place alongside the group.

sections.title: Do something together, even briefly
paragraphs: With friends, a quiz, a photo challenge or a short game can restart the conversation. With family, tell the story of an object, share a recipe or ask about a favourite holiday memory.
Offer a window rather than demanding an instant response: everyone could contribute over the weekend. For live games, confirm the time zone and duration so nobody has to miss sleep.

sections.title: Keep memories in the right circle
paragraphs: A group album is easier to revisit than a photo buried in a conversation. Add a date, place or anecdote. Before inviting a new member or reposting a photo, ask the people concerned.
Keep family memories and your friends’ moments separate: the circles may not want to share the same things. Nearly is designed around distinct relationship spaces accessible to invited members.

sections.title: Turn ‘We should meet up’ into a next step
paragraphs: Suggest two dates and a simple activity instead of waiting for the perfect weekend. If meeting is impossible, choose the next call or a remote game night. A modest, achievable date can be more useful than a big plan that never happens.

Nearly’s concept brings together friends and family spaces, questions, moments, games and a calendar. The app is announced for iOS and Android; the website’s game quiz already helps you discover an activity for your group.

faqs.question: How can I reconnect with a friend after months without contact?
faqs.answer: Send a simple message with a specific memory and an invitation that is easy to decline or reschedule. You can acknowledge the time apart without asking them to justify their silence.

faqs.question: Is Nearly only for couples?
faqs.answer: No. Nearly is designed for couples, friends and families, with a distinct private space for each connection.

title: A night with friends: games, photos and shared expenses made simple
description: Plan a night with friends in four steps: choose a game, keep photos private and work out who owes whom with a practical example.
summary: An easier evening starts with an agreed budget and an activity that suits the group. Keep photos in a chosen circle and record expenses as you go so repayments are clear.

sections.title: Before the evening: agree on the basics
paragraphs: Confirm the place, time and approximate budget. Decide whether groceries are shared by everyone or just those using them. Agreeing before a purchase avoids charging someone for an expense they did not expect.
Plan an appropriate journey home for everyone and offer alcohol-free drinks. A good evening does not require drinking or joining every game.

sections.title: Choose a game everyone can join
paragraphs: Start with a short activity and explain the rules in a minute. A group quiz or light questions can include people who know one another less well. Allow people to pass and avoid challenges that expose private information.
Nearly’s game quiz suggests an activity based on your answers. It can help you prepare; the app’s adult-only Party Mode is still coming soon.

sections.title: Decide where the photos go
paragraphs: Ask before photographing, then before publishing. Share the album only with the agreed people and accept requests to remove a picture. A private space does not replace consent.
Nearly plans a locked photo vault in Party. You can explore its presentation on the site, but do not assume that a tool makes every possible copy of an image impossible.

sections.title: Split the expenses: an example with three people
paragraphs: Alice pays €60 for groceries, Bilal pays €30 for pizza and Chloé pays nothing upfront. If the €90 is shared equally, each person owes €30. Alice has paid €30 too much, Bilal is even and Chloé owes €30: Chloé repays Alice.

Record expenses before you forget who paid and check the participants for each purchase. Nearly’s calculator is available without an account for a trial limited to three expenses. It calculates repayments; it does not make bank transfers.

faqs.question: How do you split expenses for an evening with friends?
faqs.answer: Add up shared expenses, define each person’s share and subtract what they have already paid. If a purchase concerns only part of the group, divide it among those participants.

faqs.question: Does the Nearly calculator send money?
faqs.answer: No. It shows who owes whom. You arrange the payment separately with the people involved.

title: 6 long-distance date ideas for couples
description: Find a date idea that fits your time and energy, from a photo quiz or dinner on video to a voice note walk you can do on your own schedule.
summary: For a long-distance date, pick one activity and agree how long you’ll spend on it before you call. Try a photo quiz or a conversation prompt if you have 15 minutes. If your schedules rarely overlap, exchange voice notes on the same theme and reply when you’re free.

sections.title: Two 15-minute dates for a weeknight
paragraphs: On a busy night, agree when you’ll wrap up and pick something you can start straight from your phone.
bullets: The three-photo quiz. Each choose three pictures from your week. Try to guess where your partner took theirs or what happened right after. Save the last photo for a story.

One question and a follow-up. Ask ‘What’s one detail from your day you wish I’d seen?’ Take turns answering and ask a follow-up about something in your partner’s story. End by picking a question for next time.

sections.title: Two date ideas for when you have half an hour
paragraphs: Pick a theme ahead of time and keep the prep light. A dinner date can start with whatever’s already in the cupboard.
bullets: Same ingredient, different dinner. Choose an ingredient you both have, cook something different with it and meet on video to eat. Show each other what you made and swap an idea for next time.
A short-film night. Pick a film of around ten minutes that you can both access. Count down to press play together, then compare the scenes that stayed with you.

sections.title: Two dates for when your schedules barely overlap
paragraphs: Agree a deadline that works for both of you, such as Sunday evening. Each person can take part when it suits them.
bullets: A voice note walk. While you’re out, record thirty seconds of the sounds around you and describe what’s happening. Your partner replies from a place of their choice.
A postcard for tomorrow. Send a photo and a line to read the next morning. Pick a theme such as ‘somewhere I’d take you’ and open your postcards when you wake up.

sections.title: An invitation you can send today
paragraphs: ‘Fancy a photo quiz on Thursday at 8 pm your time? Let’s do 15 minutes and bring three photos each from our week. If Thursday gets busy, we can send them on Saturday.’
If you live in different time zones, put both local times in the invitation. Let the other person choose what you do on the next date.

faqs.question: What can long-distance couples do without downloading an app?
faqs.answer: Try the three-photo quiz or the shared-ingredient dinner with the messaging app you already use. The Nearly website also has free questions for couples you can open in your browser.

faqs.question: How do you plan a long-distance date across time zones?
faqs.answer: If you’re rarely free at the same time, arrange a voice note walk or swap photo postcards before an agreed deadline. Each person can reply when they’re available.

tool.label: Pick a question for your next date

title: 5 games to play with friends on a call or in a group chat
description: Get a remote games night going with three ready-to-play games for a call and two more for friends who dip into the group chat at different times.
summary: To play with friends remotely, try forbidden words, a quick drawing round or an object hunt on a call. If friends are free at different times, run a close-up photo quiz or a caption contest in the group chat. All five games work without a separate download.

sections.title: Three games to start on a call
paragraphs: For three to six friends, start with a practice round so everyone gets the rules. Keep score if the group feels like it.
bullets: Forbidden words · 10 minutes. Get someone to guess ‘umbrella’ in thirty seconds without saying ‘rain’, ‘open’ or ‘handle’. Whoever guesses it picks the next word. This works on an audio call too.

One-minute sketch · 15 minutes. Draw ‘a cat in a suitcase’ on paper and hold it up to the camera. Give the others one minute to guess. In a bigger group, have everyone type their answer in the chat and send it on cue.

Object hunt · 15 minutes. Give everyone a prompt such as ‘something that’s been on a trip’. Allow a minute to find it and thirty seconds each to explain their choice. Anyone can describe an object from memory instead.

sections.title: Two games for the group chat
paragraphs: Set a reveal time, such as Sunday at 6 pm, so friends who see the prompt later can join in.
bullets: Mystery close-up. Post a close-up of an everyday object. Everyone sends a private guess to the person who took the photo. At the agreed time, the photographer posts the full picture and reveals the correct guesses.
Caption contest. Share a photo of an object, a landscape or an animal. Everyone writes a one-line caption. At the reveal, read them all and vote for the one you’d actually put under the photo.

sections.title: A 25-minute plan for your first games night
paragraphs: Spend five minutes welcoming everyone, then play forbidden words for ten minutes and do a ten-minute sketch round. Share the finish time upfront, especially if people are working the next day.
If the connection keeps dropping, switch to audio and put clues in the chat. Finish by posting a mystery close-up so friends who missed the call can play during the week.

faqs.question: What game can friends play remotely with their cameras off?
faqs.answer: Try forbidden words on an audio call. One person describes a word without using three related terms, and the others have thirty seconds to guess it.

faqs.question: What game works in a group chat when people reply at different times?
faqs.answer: Post a mystery close-up. Give everyone until the next day to send a private guess, then share the full photo in the group chat.

title: How to create a private family photo album
description: Decide who can see and add photos, pick an easy way to organise them and set up a family album everyone can open.
summary: To create a private family photo album, pick an invitation-only space and check its settings from an invited account. Start with ten captioned photos, then organise new ones by month or event. Agree on how photos can be passed on, especially pictures of children.

sections.title: Decide who can open the album and add photos
paragraphs: Start with a few relatives. Pick one person to manage invitations and decide who can contribute. If the service allows it, choose individual invitations over a link that anyone who receives it can open.

Use a low-stakes photo for the first test. Ask a relative to open the album on their phone and tell you what they can see, add or download. Try the link in a browser where you’re signed out to check whether a visitor can get in.

sections.title: Organise the album so it works for ten photos or a hundred
paragraphs: For everyday photos, group them by month, such as ‘November 2026’. For gatherings, use the name of the event, like ‘Lunch at Gran’s’. Stick to one main way of sorting photos.

Add one line that a relative who wasn’t there would understand. ‘Lea’s first cake’ tells more of the story than a filename. Before uploading ten shots in a row, pick the one or two that capture the moment.

sections.title: Set ground rules before sharing photos of children
paragraphs: France’s data protection authority, the CNIL, recommends sharing children’s photos privately and getting the child’s and the other parent’s agreement before posting them on social media. For your family album, agree to keep photos within the group and ask relatives to check with you before forwarding them.
Give people a simple way to ask for a picture to be taken down if they feel uncomfortable. Before adding it, check what’s visible in the background, such as an address or the name of a school.

sections.title: Get the album going in a week
paragraphs: On day one, add around ten photos and invite two relatives. Ask whoever is least comfortable with the service to find a picture and tell you where they got stuck. Fix the layout or send a short instruction before inviting the rest of the family.

At the end of the week, ask each person to add one photo and a line about it. If someone prefers to send their photo privately, ask whether they’d like you to add it for them. Keep a copy outside the shared album of the pictures that matter most to you.

faqs.question: How can I share family photos without making them public?
faqs.answer: Use an invitation-only album, turn off the public link if the service has one and check access from a signed-out browser. Ask members to check with you before forwarding a photo.

faqs.question: How can I help grandparents find family photos?
faqs.answer: Test the album on their own device and help them save a shortcut. Sort pictures by month or event and add a short caption to the ones you most want them to find.

sources.label: CNIL — Sharing photos and videos of your child on social networks

title: How to split the cost of a weekend trip with friends
description: A worked example for four friends splitting accommodation, groceries and an activity only two people joined, with the repayments calculated.
summary: To split the cost of a weekend trip, record each amount, who paid it and who took part. Divide each expense among its participants, then compare what each person paid with their total share. Those who paid less than their share repay those who covered more.

sections.title: Agree how to split costs before you book
paragraphs: Share the cost of the accommodation per person and ask everyone to confirm before putting down a deposit. Decide whether to split accommodation equally or by the number of nights each person stays. Bring it up while everyone can still adjust their plans.

For groceries, transport and activities, record who took part in each expense. A museum booking for two is split between those two people. For personal purchases, ask for a separate receipt or take those items off the shared total.

sections.title: A worked example with four friends and an activity for two
paragraphs: Camille pays €240 for accommodation and Sam pays €60 for groceries. Both expenses cover Camille, Sam, Lou and Noa. Lou also pays €36 for an activity that only Lou and Noa attend.
bullets: Accommodation and groceries: €300 ÷ 4 = €75 each.
Activity: €36 ÷ 2 = €18 each for Lou and Noa.
Final shares: Camille and Sam owe €75 each. Lou and Noa owe €93 each.
Repayments: Sam sends Camille €15, Lou sends her €57 and Noa sends her €93. Camille gets back the €165 she paid above her share.

sections.title: Try the worked example in the Nearly calculator
paragraphs: The website demo takes three expenses. Add all four friends and create rows for ‘Accommodation’, ‘Groceries’ and ‘Activity’. Enter the amount, who paid it and who took part for each one. Select only Lou and Noa for the activity.

If accommodation costs €240 in total and you already put down an €80 deposit, count either the full amount paid by one person or the €80 deposit and the €160 balance with their respective payers. Check the amounts and participants together before sending any money.

faqs.question: How do you split an expense when only two friends took part?
faqs.answer: Divide it between the two friends who took part. In the Nearly calculator, enter who paid and select just those two people as participants for that expense.

faqs.question: How do you work out who owes whom when several friends paid?
faqs.answer: For each person, subtract their total share from what they paid upfront. A positive balance is what they should receive. A negative balance is what they need to repay.

tool.label: Calculate repayments for your weekend trip
